lec05kp02-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp02-u01-p1-title.text: One line fails, so ask two lines first and then decide

lec05kp02-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p1-bridge.text: The previous KP picked out A with a strip between two lines. How can neurons make these two decisions?

lec05kp02-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-input-lines
lec05kp02-u01-p1-fig1.text: The XOR points with two parallel lines g1=x1+x2-0.5 (teal) and g2=x1+x2-1.5 (violet).

image.alt: The XOR points with two parallel lines g1=x1+x2-0.5 (teal) and g2=x1+x2-1.5 (violet).

lec05kp02-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp02-u01-p1-c1.text: **Idea**: one line cannot answer 'A or B?' directly, so first ask two small questions and classify from the answers.

lec05kp02-u01-p1-term:隱藏層.name: term:Hidden layer
lec05kp02-u01-p1-term:隱藏層.text: **Hidden layer and output layer**: the row of lines that asks the small questions is the hidden layer, and the last plane that classifies is the output layer. Inputs only supply coordinates and are not a layer: a two-layer network is a hidden layer plus an output layer.

lec05kp02-u01-p1-q.name: u01-p1-q
lec05kp02-u01-p1-q.text: **To answer**: what does each of the two lines ask?

lec05kp02-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp02-u01-p2-title.text: Each line asks: is the point on the positive side? Record one bit

lec05kp02-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p2-bridge.text: To ask two small questions, use two parallel lines and ask each: is the point on its positive side? How do we record each answer?

lec05kp02-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-input-sides
lec05kp02-u01-p2-fig1.text: The same figure with the positive side of each line tinted and marked by an arrow; where the tints overlap both lines are on their positive side.

image.alt: The same figure with the positive side of each line tinted and marked by an arrow; where the tints overlap both lines are on their positive side.

lec05kp02-u01-p2-term:位元.name: term:Bit
lec05kp02-u01-p2-term:位元.text: **Bit**: a point on the positive side of a line (score $>0$) gets 1, otherwise 0.

lec05kp02-u01-p2-term:階梯規則.name: term:Step rule
lec05kp02-u01-p2-term:階梯規則.text: **Step rule**: a positive score gives 1, anything else gives 0 (exactly 0 also gives 0).

lec05kp02-u01-p2-term:隱藏編碼.name: term:Hidden code
lec05kp02-u01-p2-term:隱藏編碼.text: **Two parallel lines**: $g_1=x_1+x_2-0.5$ and $g_2=x_1+x_2-1.5$. The two bits written together, $\mathbf y=[y_1,y_2]$, form the **hidden code**, like two position labels attached to the point.

lec05kp02-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p3-bridge.text: Each line asks whether the point is on its positive side and records one bit. Walk $(0,1)$ through: what hidden code does it get?

lec05kp02-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-bits-example
lec05kp02-u01-p3-fig1.text: Example point (0,1): g1=0.5>0 gives y1=1 and g2=-0.5<=0 gives y2=0, so its code is (1,0).

image.alt: Example point (0,1): g1=0.5>0 gives y1=1 and g2=-0.5<=0 gives y2=0, so its code is (1,0).

lec05kp02-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p4-bridge.text: Walking $(0,1)$ through gave scores 0.5 and −0.5 and the hidden code $(1,0)$. What are the scores and codes of all four points?

lec05kp02-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-bands
lec05kp02-u01-p4-fig1.text: The two lines cut the plane into three bands labelled with the codes (0,0), (1,0) and (1,1); both A points lie in the middle band (1,0).

image.alt: The two lines cut the plane into three bands labelled with the codes (0,0), (1,0) and (1,1); both A points lie in the middle band (1,0).

lec05kp02-u01-p4-note.name: u01-p4-note
lec05kp02-u01-p4-note.text: The two A points $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ get the **same code** $(1,0)$: four inputs occupy only three locations. Does this lose information?

lec05kp02-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp02-u01-p5-title.text: In the plane of codes, one line separates A from B

lec05kp02-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p5-bridge.text: Four points occupy three locations and the two A points share one. Can A and B still be separated by these codes?

lec05kp02-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-hidden-plane
lec05kp02-u01-p5-fig1.text: Hidden space (y1,y2): (0,0) is B, (1,0) is A (two merged inputs), (1,1) is B, and (0,1) is empty; the output line y2=y1-0.5 separates A from B.

image.alt: Hidden space (y1,y2): (0,0) is B, (1,0) is A (two merged inputs), (1,1) is B, and (0,1) is empty; the output line y2=y1-0.5 separates A from B.

lec05kp02-u01-p5-term:隱藏空間.name: term:Hidden space
lec05kp02-u01-p5-term:隱藏空間.text: **Hidden space**: replace every point by its code $(y_1,y_2)$ and draw it in a new plane: $(0,0)$ is B, $(1,0)$ is A (two merged inputs) and $(1,1)$ is B; the hollow $(0,1)$ means no input lands there.

lec05kp02-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp02-u01-p5-c2.text: **The output line**: $g_{\text{out}}=y_1-y_2-0.5$, the line is $y_2=y_1-0.5$; $g_{\text{out}}>0$ (below the line) means A.

lec05kp02-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp02-u01-p5-c3.text: Merging the two A points does not matter, because they are the same class.

lec05kp02-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp02-u01-p6-title.text: Output layer check: predictions (0,1,1,0) are exactly XOR

lec05kp02-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p6-bridge.text: The output layer draws one line in the plane of codes. Computed point by point, what are its predictions?

lec05kp02-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-hidden-scores
lec05kp02-u01-p6-fig1.text: Output scores at the three hidden locations: -0.5 at (0,0), 0.5 at (1,0) and -0.5 at (1,1); only (1,0) is positive, so class A.

image.alt: Output scores at the three hidden locations: -0.5 at (0,0), 0.5 at (1,0) and -0.5 at (1,1); only (1,0) is positive, so class A.

lec05kp02-u01-p6-res.name: u01-p6-res
lec05kp02-u01-p6-res.text: The predictions for the four inputs are $(0,1,1,0)$, exactly XOR: 4 of 4 correct. This checks these four points; it is not an accuracy on new data.

lec05kp02-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp02-u01-p7-title.text: Back in the original plane: the whole network is the strip between two lines

lec05kp02-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p7-bridge.text: The output layer classified the four points. Back in the original $(x_1,x_2)$ plane, what does the whole network look like?

lec05kp02-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-strip-net
lec05kp02-u01-p7-fig1.text: Back in the original plane: the region y1=1 and y2=0 is the strip between the two lines, with both A points inside and both B points outside.

image.alt: Back in the original plane: the region y1=1 and y2=0 is the strip between the two lines, with both A points inside and both B points outside.

lec05kp02-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp02-u01-p7-c1.text: **Translate back**: $y_1=1$ and $y_2=0$ means $g_1>0$ and $g_2\le0$, that is $x_1+x_2>0.5$ and $x_1+x_2\le1.5$.

lec05kp02-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp02-u01-p7-c2.text: **This is the strip of the previous KP**: the hidden layer makes the two decisions and the output layer asks for both; in the original plane the network selects the strip between the lines, with both A points inside.

lec05kp02-u01-p7-c3.name: u01-p7-c3
lec05kp02-u01-p7-c3.text: **Next**: if we add more hidden lines, what do they cut? (the next KP)

lec05kp02-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp02-u01-p8-title.text: Merging the same class is fine; merging different classes is not

lec05kp02-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p8-bridge.text: The whole network is a strip and merging the two A points is harmless. Is every merge harmless? When does it go wrong?

lec05kp02-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-merge-bad
lec05kp02-u01-p8-fig1.text: Schematic: if an A and a B receive the same code (1,1), marked by a red ring, no output line can separate them.

image.alt: Schematic: if an A and a B receive the same code (1,1), marked by a red ring, no output line can separate them.

lec05kp02-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp02-u01-p8-c1.text: **Merging one class is harmless**: here the two A points merge and the output layer still separates them. Note that $y_1,y_2$ are only 'on the positive side?' bits, not class probabilities.

lec05kp02-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp02-u01-p8-c2.text: **Merging different classes is bad**: if points of different classes receive the same code, no output line can separate them and later decisions cannot recover.

lec05kp02-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp02-u01-p8-c3.text: **Next**: with more hidden lines, can a two-layer network separate any labelling? (the next KP)

lec05kp02-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp02-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: practice, change the output bias to +0.5

lec05kp02-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p9-bridge.text: Merging different classes makes the output layer fail. What if only the output bias changes from $-0.5$ to $+0.5$: what are the four predictions?

lec05kp02-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-bias-line
lec05kp02-u01-p9-fig1.text: Practice figure: the three hidden locations with the output line y2=y1+0.5 (output bias changed to +0.5).

image.alt: Practice figure: the three hidden locations with the output line y2=y1+0.5 (output bias changed to +0.5).

lec05kp02-u01-p9-q1.name: u01-p9-q1
lec05kp02-u01-p9-q1.text: **Question 1**: with $g_{\text{out}}=y_1-y_2+0.5$, what are the predictions for the four inputs?

lec05kp02-u01-p9-h1.name: u01-p9-h1
lec05kp02-u01-p9-h1.text: **Hint**: keep the hidden codes $(0,0),(1,0),(1,0),(1,1)$ and recompute only the output scores.

lec05kp02-u01-p9-q2.name: u01-p9-q2
lec05kp02-u01-p9-q2.text: **Question 2**: which different inputs are merged, and why does the merge cause no conflict?

lec05kp02-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p10-bridge.text: The practice changed the output bias to $+0.5$ and recomputed only the output scores. What are the four predictions?

lec05kp02-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-bias-plus
lec05kp02-u01-p10-fig1.text: With the output bias +0.5 all three locations have positive scores and are predicted A; the two B locations (0,0) and (1,1) are circled in red as wrong.

image.alt: With the output bias +0.5 all three locations have positive scores and are predicted A; the two B locations (0,0) and (1,1) are circled in red as wrong.

lec05kp02-u01-p10-a3.name: u01-p10-a3
lec05kp02-u01-p10-a3.text: **③ Predictions**: all three scores are positive, so all four inputs are predicted A.

lec05kp02-u01-p10-a4.name: u01-p10-a4
lec05kp02-u01-p10-a4.text: **④ Check**: XOR is B, A, A, B, so the two B inputs are predicted A: 2 errors. The bias moved the line so it no longer separates B from A.

lec05kp02-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp02-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: the steps cannot be removed, or the network stays linear

lec05kp02-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp02-u01-p11-bridge.text: The output bias cannot be changed freely. What about the steps in the hidden layer? If we remove them, what does the output score become?

lec05kp02-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp02-no-step
lec05kp02-u01-p11-fig1.text: Without the steps the output score equals 0.5 everywhere, so the whole plane is predicted A; the two B points (0,0) and (1,1) are circled in red as wrong.

image.alt: Without the steps the output score equals 0.5 everywhere, so the whole plane is predicted A; the two B points (0,0) and (1,1) are circled in red as wrong.

lec05kp02-u01-p11-b4.name: u01-p11-b4
lec05kp02-u01-p11-b4.text: **④ Result**: all points predicted A, 2 XOR errors. Linear combinations stay linear, so nonlinearity needs the steps.

steps.label: Encode and classify
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Rewritten under CLARITY.md C12 to C18: plain words before terms, titles that state the point, pages linked by questions, a figure on every spatial page. These notes are public with the file and contain no student IDs, grades or exam questions.

steps.label: Two small questions
steps.speakerNotes: The previous KP ended with two parallel lines enclosing a strip that contains the A points of XOR; this page starts turning that into a network. One line cannot answer 'A or B?' directly, so we first ask two small questions and classify from the two answers. The row of lines that asks the small questions is the hidden layer and the plane that makes the final classification is the output layer. The input nodes only supply the coordinates x1 and x2 and are not a layer, so a two-layer network here is one hidden layer plus one output layer; check how other texts count layers. The figure shows the same four XOR points with the two parallel lines g1 and g2. Next, page 2 shows what each line asks.

steps.label: One bit per line
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page decided to ask two small questions; here we say exactly what each line asks: is the point on the positive side of this line? The positive side is where the score is greater than 0; if yes the answer is recorded as 1 and otherwise 0, and this 0 or 1 is a bit; a point exactly on the line has score 0 and also gets 0. The two lines are g1 = x1+x2-0.5 and g2 = x1+x2-1.5, and in the figure teal and violet tint their positive sides with arrows pointing to them. The two bits together, (y1, y2), are the hidden code. The rule that turns a score into 0 or 1 is the step rule; it is nonlinear, and the last extension page shows why it cannot be removed. Next, page 3 walks one point through.

steps.label: Walk through (0,1)
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page defined bits and the hidden code; here we walk (0,1) through. Substituting (0,1) into the first line gives g1 = 0 + 1 - 0.5 = 0.5, which is greater than 0, so y1 = 1; the second line gives g2 = 0 + 1 - 1.5 = -0.5, which is not greater than 0, so y2 = 0. The hidden code is (1,0). The star in the figure is this point and the labels show its two scores and two bits. Let the students repeat it with (0,0). The flow on the right reads top to bottom: input, two scores, step rule, hidden code. Next, page 4 computes all four points.

steps.label: The four codes
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page walked (0,1); here we compute all four points: (0,0) has scores -0.5 and -1.5 and code (0,0); (0,1) and (1,0) both have scores 0.5 and -0.5 and code (1,0); (1,1) has scores 1.5 and 0.5 and code (1,1). In the figure the plane is cut into three bands: the lower one has code (0,0), the middle one (1,0) and the upper one (1,1). Note that both A points lie in the middle band and therefore share one code; four inputs occupy three locations. Does that lose information? Next, page 5 looks at the plane of codes.

steps.label: A line on the codes
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed the two A points sharing a code; here we look at the plane of codes: replace every point by its code (y1, y2) and draw it in a new plane. (0,0) is B, (1,0) is A (two inputs merged into one location), (1,1) is B and (0,1) is hollow because no input reaches it. In this new plane the line y2 = y1 - 0.5 separates A from B: below it the score y1 - y2 - 0.5 is positive, class A. Merging the two A points does not matter because they are the same class; merging different classes would be the problem, as page 8 shows. This line is the output layer. Next, page 6 checks it point by point.

steps.label: Check the output
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page drew the output line; here we compute the output score y1 - y2 - 0.5 point by point: (0,0) gives -0.5, class B; (1,0) gives 0.5, class A, which stands for both A inputs; (1,1) gives -0.5, class B. So the predictions for the four inputs are 0, 1, 1, 0, exactly XOR, four of four correct. The figure shows the output score beside each location. Stress that this checks the construction on four points and is not an accuracy estimate on new data; these weights were not learned automatically but come from the source's construction. Next, page 7 turns the whole network back into the original plane.

steps.label: The net is a strip
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page checked the output layer; here we turn the whole network back into the original (x1, x2) plane: y1 = 1 and y2 = 0 means x1+x2 is greater than 0.5 and at most 1.5, the strip between the two parallel lines. This is the condition 0.5 < s <= 1.5 that ended the previous KP: the hidden layer makes the two decisions and the output layer asks for both. In the figure the blue strip contains the two A points and the two B points lie outside; it is the same picture as the strip of the previous KP, so let students compare. Note that the output line is drawn in the plane of codes, not directly on the original plot. Next, page 8 discusses the limits of this construction.

steps.label: Limits of merging
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the whole network is a strip and that merging the two A points caused no trouble. This page asks whether every merge is harmless. Merging one class is harmless because the merged points still have the same label; but if points of different classes receive the same code, no output line can separate them. The figure is a schematic with an A and a B both at (1,1) and a red ring marking the conflict. Another common mistake is to read y1 and y2 as class probabilities; they are only 'on the positive side?' bits. This construction proves that XOR is representable, while other tasks must first check that the hidden codes can be separated by the output layer. Next comes the following KP: with more hidden lines, can one output layer separate any labelling?

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said that only merging different classes is a problem; this page asks students to check by themselves. Keep the hidden codes and change only the output bias from -0.5 to +0.5. The hint is to keep the codes (0,0), (1,0), (1,0), (1,1) and recompute the output score y1 - y2 + 0.5. The figure draws the new output line y2 = y1 + 0.5; ask the students to decide first which side each location lies on and then compare with the solution on the next page. Question 2 asks which inputs are merged and why that causes no conflict; hint: look at their labels.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed question 1 and this page is its full solution: the formula is g_out = y1 - y2 + 0.5; substituting gives 0.5 at (0,0), 1.5 at (1,0) and 0.5 at (1,1); all three are positive, so all four inputs are predicted A; XOR is B, A, A, B, so the two B inputs are wrong, 2 errors, marked by the red rings. The output bias cannot be changed freely: it shifts the line and can put B and A back on the same side. This is the same constant term as in the first KP. Next, the last page asks what happens if we remove the steps.

steps.label: Extension: steps
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the bias cannot be changed freely; this page asks whether the steps can be dropped. Without the steps the hidden outputs are the scores themselves, y1 = x1+x2-0.5 and y2 = x1+x2-1.5; substituting into the output score gives (x1+x2-0.5) - (x1+x2-1.5) - 0.5, where x1 and x2 cancel completely and leave the constant 0.5, so every point is predicted A and XOR has 2 errors. The reason is that a combination of linear expressions is linear again, however many layers there are, so the nonlinearity can only come from operations such as the step. This is an added derivation, checked by program. KP02 ends here; next comes the following KP: what regions do more hidden lines cut?
